title: Member initializer lists
learningGoals: explain why const members need it

youtube.title: C++ Member Initializer Lists | C++ Programming EP 54
youtube.description: In this episode you will write a member initializer list, explain why const members need it and avoid the order warning, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Member initializer lists · 1:25 An initializer list · 2:19 Order of events · 2:55 Second program · 4:06 Recap · 4:36 Bug of the Day · 5:31 Challenge · 5:57 Next episode

thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a checklist stuck to a toolbox

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we learn the right way to set up members. The colon list runs before the body, and some members need it.

scenes.onScreen: "Member initializer lists": numbered lines (1. The list runs before the constructor body; 2. Const and reference members must use it; 3. Members start in the order they are declared) and an analogy card: a school bag checklist: pack things in the order of the list on the door
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A member initializer list sits after the constructor brackets. It starts with a colon. It builds each member directly, before the body runs. Const members and reference members must use it. Members are always built in the order of their declaration, not in the order of your list. Think of a school bag. You pack in the order of the checklist on the door. There is a difference between building a member and assigning to it. In the body of a constructor, the members are already built, and then you change them. In the initializer list, each member is built with the right value at once. For a string, this saves work. For a const member, it is the only way.
points: The list runs before the constructor body
Const and reference members must use it
Members start in the order they are declared

scenes.onScreen: initlist.cpp: a constructor sets two members before its body runs
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 10] The colon starts the initializer list. [HL 10] Each entry names a member, and gives it a value in round brackets. [HL 11] The body runs after the list. [HL 17] We make a book. The list runs first, then the body prints Book made. [HL 18] Then show prints the title and the pages. [HL 10] The list sits between the brackets and the body. Title and pages each get their value in parentheses. [HL 11] The body runs after the list. This message proves that all members are already built. [HL 17] The object gets its name and its page count in one step.

scenes.onScreen: a flow: list, body, object ready
scenes.animation: Steps drop in left to right with a pop; connecting arrows draw on; the active step glows butter
scenes.narration: Follow the order. First, the members are built. They get the values from the list. Then the body runs. Only then is the object ready for use. Notice the order of events. First all members are built, in the order of the declaration. Then the body runs. So the body is the place for extra work, not for setting values.

diagram.caption: a flow: list, body, object ready

scenes.onScreen: constmember.cpp: a const member can only be set by the list
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 5] The id is const. It must never change. [HL 9] A const member can only get its value in the list. Setting it in the body is too late. [HL 14] We make a ticket with id one hundred and one, and price fifty. [HL 15] The output shows both numbers. [HL 5] This member is const. After it is built, it can never change. [HL 9] The list gives it its value, so there is no assignment. [HL 14] The ticket gets id one hundred and one, and price fifty.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as constmember dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints one hundred one, then fifty. The id can never change after the ticket is made. That is the idea of const.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. The initializer list sits between the colon and the body. Two. It builds each member directly. Three. Const and reference members must use the list. Four. Members are built in declaration order. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: The initializer list sits between the colon and the body.
Const and reference members must use the list.
Members are built in declaration order.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: A list in the wrong order
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the g++ warning appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the warning goes away with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. The list names second before first. But members are always built in the order of the declaration. The compiler warns about the wrong order. Write the list in the same order as the members. Members are built in the order of the declaration. If your list says price first and id second, the compiler still builds id first. Warnings with the Wall flag point this out. Keep both in the same order, and you avoid surprises.

scenes.onScreen: The initializer list is like a packing list. It never lets the constructor forget its socks.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: The initializer list is like a packing list. It never lets the constructor forget its socks.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: use an initializer list with a const

scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a class called Student with a const roll number and a name. Use an initializer list. Hint: a const member must be set in the initializer list, so the body can stay empty. Write your answer in the comments.

bug.error:
Compiler output (a warning, the program still builds):

initlist.cpp: In constructor 'Pair::Pair(int, int)':
initlist.cpp:6:9: warning: 'Pair::second_' will be initialized after [-Wreorder]
    6 |     int second_;
      |         ^~~~~~~
bug.why: The compiler builds members in the order of the declaration. A list in a different order is misleading, and it can cause real bugs.

challengeAnswer: Declare a const int for the roll number and a string for the name. In the constructor, write a colon, then each member with its value in round brackets.
